Slides (black), the lecture notes (green — study guide written from the lecture by Mohammed Alessa, Mohammed Alsalamah & Abdulrahman Alomar) and every gift (red). Aldughaither has no urology chapter. This year the lecture is renal colic only; older exams also asked about haematuria, urological trauma and UTI from the previous "Presentation & investigation of urinary tract problems" lecture — those questions are in section 7 with added background.

King Saud University logo and kidney illustration (title slide) (2)
  • The whole lecture follows one patient through three stages: (1) uncomplicated colic → hydration · analgesia · medical expulsive therapy; (2) obstructed + infected kidney → cultures → broad-spectrum antibiotics → urgent urine diversion (DJ stent); (3) infection cleared (negative culture) → definitive stone treatment chosen by site and size.
  • One-line summary: uncomplicated colic → conservative. Obstruction + infection → drain first, antibiotics alongside. Infection gone → remove the stone.

1. The case — history & examination

  • Case: a 24-year-old male presented with left flank pain for 2 days. Next?
Flank pain; history checklist (decorative) (2)
  • History: pain · urinary symptoms · eliminate differential diagnosis.
  • Characterise the pain: onset (sudden?), duration, severity (often 10/10), radiation loin → groin, aggravating/relieving factors, relation to movement. Urinary symptoms: haematuria, dysuria, frequency, urgency — their absence does not exclude a stone. Eliminate the differentials: GI symptoms, fever (infection changes everything), chest, gynae and testicular symptoms.
  • Physical examination: general examination · abdominal examination · costovertebral angle tenderness.

Abdominal examination; costovertebral angle tenderness (angle between the 12th rib and the spine)

  • General: vital signs — fever, tachycardia, hypotension point to sepsis. Abdomen: peritonism/guarding, masses, a pulsatile mass (aneurysm), palpable bladder. CVA tenderness localises the problem to the kidney.

Differential diagnosis

  • Radiculitis (pseudo-renal) · leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm · pneumonia · myocardial infarction · ovarian pathology (twisted ovarian cyst) · acute appendicitis · testicular torsion · IBD (Crohn's, UC) · diverticulitis · ectopic pregnancy · burst peptic ulcer · bowel obstruction.
  • Can't-miss mimics: older patient with a "first ever" renal colic → think leaking AAA (feel for a pulsatile mass, check BP) · woman of reproductive age → pregnancy test (ectopic), consider ovarian torsion · young male with groin pain → always examine the testes (torsion) · referred upper-abdominal pain with risk factors → ECG for MI; peritonism → perforated ulcer. Radicular pain varies with movement.

The case, continued

  • Pain radiating to groin. No aggravating or relieving factors. Sudden. 10/10. No urinary symptoms · not related to movement · no GI symptoms · no fever · left flank tenderness. Next?
  • Sudden 10/10 loin-to-groin pain = acute ureteric obstruction by a stone. Not related to movement argues against musculoskeletal/radicular pain. No fever = uncomplicated colic (for now).
  • 40-year-old, sudden right flank pain radiating to the lower abdomen, CVA tenderness → right ureteric stone. 435 ×4

2. Investigations

  • CBC · renal profile · urine analysis · imaging (which one?).
  • CBC: raised WBC = infection → changes management. Renal profile: renal impairment is an indication to intervene. Urinalysis: haematuria supports a stone; pyuria/nitrites suggest infection (send culture).

KUB plain films

IVU (intravenous urogram)

  • Gold standard: CT without contrast.
Trophy ("gold standard" slide decoration) (1)
ModalityWhat it showsStrengthsLimitations
KUBRadio-opaque stones (calcium)Cheap, quick, low dose; follow-up of a known radio-opaque stoneMisses radiolucent stones (uric acid, xanthine); bowel gas and bone overlap
USHydronephrosis; renal stonesNo radiation — first choice in pregnancy and childrenPoor at seeing ureteric stones; operator dependent
IVUContrast excretion → level of obstruction, delayed functionAnatomy and function togetherIV contrast, radiation, slow — largely replaced by CT
MRUDilated system; stone as a filling defectNo ionising radiationStones poorly seen; costly
CT without contrast — gold standardVirtually all stones: size, site, density; hydronephrosisMost sensitive and specific; detects alternative diagnosesRadiation dose
  • Why non-contrast? It sees stones invisible on KUB (uric acid), and contrast is bright and would hide the stone. It gives what the treatment decision needs: site + size. Typical adult → non-contrast CT; pregnant or child → US first; known radio-opaque stone follow-up → KUB.
  • Renal stones — investigation of choice → CT (non-contrast). 441 ×2
  • Coronal non-contrast CT (picture) — diagnosis → kidney stone. 439

3. Treatment of uncomplicated colic

  • Hydration · analgesia · medical expulsion therapy. When do you admit/intervene?
  • Hydration: fluids / IV fluids if vomiting. Analgesia: NSAIDs first line (if no contraindication); opioids for breakthrough pain. Medical expulsive therapy: α1-blocker (e.g. tamsulosin) relaxes distal ureteric smooth muscle to help the stone pass.
  • Indications to admit/intervene: infection · renal impairment · persistent nausea and vomiting · persistent pain not responding to oral analgesia · failure of medical therapy.
  • Memory hook — "I Really Need Proper Fixing": Infection · Renal impairment (raised creatinine, single kidney, bilateral obstruction) · Nausea & vomiting · Pain not controlled orally · Failure of medical therapy.
  • 25-year-old, 2 days of left ureteric colic, 4 mm radio-opaque distal ureteric stone → initial management adequate analgesia and hydration. 438 ×6
Source key vs the doctor's pathway: a 6-mm ureteric stone in a woman with flank pain and no complication was keyed "ureteroscopy". The doctor's pathway for uncomplicated colic is hydration, analgesia and medical expulsive therapy, intervening only for the five indications above — so the answer here is conservative. Choose URS when an indication is present (or MET fails).
  • 25-year-old woman, left flank pain, CT: 6 mm left ureteric stone, no complication → conservative (analgesia, hydration, MET). 438

4. The obstructed, infected kidney

  • Case: same patient presented with fever and increased left flank pain. CBC: elevated WBC. Renal profile: normal. CT: same. Next?
  • Treatment: hydration · analgesia · UA and C/S and blood C/S · broad-spectrum antibiotics · urine diversion.
  • Danger: infection behind an obstructing stone = pus under pressure. The patient can become septic quickly — antibiotics alone are not enough; the kidney must be decompressed urgently. Cultures are taken before antibiotics; narrow once results return.
  • Urine diversion: DJ stent · nephrostomy.

Percutaneous nephrostomy and double-J ureteric stent

  • Why? Antibiotic levels are low with obstruction · sepsis if definitive therapy.
Bacteria (decorative) (1)
  • Antibiotics alone fail — drug levels are low in an obstructed system that isn't draining. Definitive treatment now → sepsis — manipulating a stone in an infected obstructed system pushes bacteria into the blood. Rule: drain first, treat the stone later — after a negative urine culture.
DJ (double-J) ureteric stentPercutaneous nephrostomy
RouteRetrograde — cystoscopy, up the ureter past the stoneNeedle and tube through the flank into the renal pelvis (US/fluoroscopy)
DrainageInternal, into the bladderExternal, into a bag (output measurable)
AnaesthesiaUsually general / spinalUsually local
PlusesNo external bagDoesn't need to pass the stone; useful when retrograde access fails
MinusesStent symptoms (frequency, urgency, haematuria, flank pain on voiding); must be removed laterExternal bag; dislodgement; bleeding
  • 55-year-old, fever, chills, flank pain, pyuria, bacteraemia, sepsis, 6-mm obstructing ureteric stone → percutaneous nephrostomy + IV antibiotics. 442 ×2

5. Definitive treatment

  • Case: same patient underwent DJ insertion and 2 weeks later urine culture was negative. Next?
Operating theatre (decorative) (1)
  • ESWL · URS · PCNL · cystolitholapaxy.

Shock wave lithotripsy (SWL) and a lithotripter

QR codes and video frames — ESWL: youtube.com/watch?v=0hKRYVrlfdI · URS: youtube.com/watch?v=ayCH5cc0y1M (4)
ProcedureHow it worksApproach
ESWLShock waves generated outside the body are focused on the stone (X-ray/US); fragments pass in the urineNon-invasive
URSScope via urethra and bladder up the ureter; stone fragmented (laser) and/or removed (basket); a flexible scope reaches stones in the kidneyEndoscopic, retrograde
PCNLTract from the flank directly into the kidney; stone fragmented and extractedPercutaneous — large renal stones
CystolitholapaxyCystoscope via the urethra; bladder stone crushed and washed outEndoscopic, transurethral

Choosing by site and size

  • Bladder stone: cystolitholapaxy.
  • Ureteric stone: mid and lower ureter → ureteroscopy > ESWL. Upper ureter: > 1 cm → ureteroscopy > ESWL; < 1 cm → ureteroscopy or ESWL.

Rigid ureteroscope reaching a ureteric stone; patient positioned for ESWL

  • Renal stone: > 2 cm → PCNL. < 2 cm → URS vs ESWL.

PCNL — prone percutaneous access into the kidney

  • Two numbers to remember: kidney 2 cm (above → PCNL; below → URS vs ESWL) · upper ureter 1 cm (above → URS beats ESWL; below → either). Everywhere lower in the ureter, URS wins. Ureteric thirds are defined by the sacroiliac joint: upper (above), middle (over), lower (below).
  • Left renal stone, KUB shows a staghorn (large branched) stone → percutaneous nephrolithotomy. 438 ×5
  • 40-year-old, stable, ureteric stone with hydronephrosis, no infection — among nephrectomy, open surgery, antibiotics → ESWL. 442

6. Types of stones

StoneForms in urine that is…On X-ray (KUB)Clinical note
Calcium saltsAlkaline — need high pHRadio-opaqueCommonest stones by far
Uric acidAcidic — need low pHRadio-lucentInvisible on KUB, seen on non-contrast CT
Mg ammonium PO4 (struvite)Alkaline — need high pHFaint radio-opaque"Infection stones" — urease-producing bacteria (e.g. Proteus); staghorn calculi
CystineAcidic — need low pHFaint radio-opaqueInherited cystinuria
XanthineAcidic — need low pHRadio-lucentRare
  • Memory hooks — the acid trio: uric acid · cystine · xanthine form in acidic urine; calcium and struvite in alkaline urine. Radiolucent = U and X (uric acid, xanthine) — a normal plain film doesn't exclude a stone.
  • Flank pain to the groin, haematuria, recurrent UTIs, alkaline urine with urease-producing bacteria → struvite stone. 441
  • 1 cm renal pelvis stone on US, not seen on KUB → uric acid. 429

7. Other urology questions asked (previous "Presentation & investigation" lecture)

Haematuria

Added explanationPainless gross haematuria in an adult — especially a smoker over 40 — is urothelial (bladder) cancer until proven otherwise. Work-up = upper tract imaging (CT urography; IVU in older keys) + cystoscopy — CT can miss flat bladder tumours, so a normal CT urogram must be followed by cystoscopy. Urine cytology helps.
  • 60-year-old with painless gross haematuria, urine full of RBCs → urothelial carcinoma. 436
  • 55-year-old heavy smoker with occasional gross painless haematuria → next CT (urography). 438
  • Same patient, no UTI, CT urogram normal → next cystoscopy. 437 ×4
  • Painless macroscopic haematuria — imaging of choice among US, MRI, IVU, isotope → intravenous urography (CT urography replaces it today). 429
Added explanationA solid renal mass in a fit patient without metastases is renal cell carcinoma until proven otherwise → surgery (radical nephrectomy; partial nephrectomy when technically feasible, especially for tumours ≤ 7 cm). RCC is resistant to conventional chemotherapy and radiotherapy.
  • 55-year-old woman, solid 6 cm left renal mass, no metastasis, normal other kidney → radical nephrectomy. 429

Urinary tract infection

Added explanationThe most reliable urine sample is suprapubic aspiration (any growth is significant — it bypasses the urethra); a catheter specimen is next; midstream is the routine one. Sterile pyuria (white cells, negative culture) → think TB, stones, tumour, recent antibiotics.
  • Most reliable urine specimen to diagnose UTI → suprapubic aspiration. 436
  • Routine check: turbid urine, many WBCs, negative culture (sterile pyuria) — among tumour, stricture, retention, trauma → tumour. 434 ×2

Urological trauma

Added explanationBlood at the urethral meatus (pelvic fracture, straddle injury) = urethral injury → retrograde (ascending) urethrogram before any catheter; if retention, a suprapubic catheter. Bladder rupture on cystogram: extraperitoneal = flame-shaped contrast confined around the bladder (pelvic fracture) → catheter drainage; intraperitoneal = contrast outlining bowel loops (blow to a full bladder) → surgical repair. Ureteric injury after pelvic surgery → clear fluid from the drain with low urine output (check drain creatinine).
  • 30-year-old after MVA with blood at the urethral meatus → retrograde urethrogram. 429
  • 7-year-old, straddle injury, urethral bleeding, difficulty voiding → ascending urethrogram. 436
  • Woman after MVA, cystogram with contrast confined around the bladder → extraperitoneal bladder injury. 438
  • 2 days after emergency hysterectomy, drain 800 mL/day of clear fluid, urine 700 mL/day → ureteral injury. 436
Added explanationDelayed haematuria 2–3 weeks after renal trauma treated conservatively is classically from a renal artery pseudoaneurysm or AV fistula (clots cause colic) → CT angiography and angio-embolization.
  • 3 weeks after a managed grade 3 renal injury: haematuria and left renal colic → renal artery (pseudo)aneurysm. 436 ×3
